LR-001  |  Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, SC 2000, c 5

rows: Canada | Binding federal law when applicable | Status: in force

"An organization may collect, use or disclose personal information only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider are appropriate in the circumstances." Section 7(1)(b) requires both reasonable expectation that knowledge/consent would compromise availability or accuracy and a reasonable investigation purpose. Section 7(2)(d) permits use only of information collected under specified subsection 7(1) exceptions; it is not an independent collection authority. Section 7.1(3) disapplies listed collection/use exceptions for information obtained by unauthorized computer access.

The consent exception does not remove the appropriate-purpose, necessity, source-authority, access, breach or accountability requirements; each transaction/search pathway needs a recorded legal basis.

Applies to: Counterparty or transaction evidence retrieval; user-export ingestion; access/correction; breach response; output and source governance.

PIA-001 lawful-basis gate; SR-001 source approval; LOG-001; PRIV-001; IR-001; OPS-001.

3. Applicable human-rights framework
3.1 Alberta Human Rights Act

[F] Section 4 prohibits denial of, or discrimination in relation to, goods, services, accommodation or facilities customarily available to the public because of any of fifteen listed grounds. Section 11 permits a respondent to show that an alleged contravention was reasonable and justifiable in the circumstances. Whether a particular 4ormIQ deployment is itself a service customarily available to the public, and how the closing words concerning another person or class apply to transaction participants, are fact-specific counsel questions. [C]
Authorities: [S01] Alberta Human Rights Act, RSA 2000, c A-25.5, ss.4 and 11 | [S02] Alberta Human Rights Commission, Protected grounds
3.2 Prima facie discrimination

[F] Moore para.33 requires: (1) a protected characteristic; (2) an adverse impact in the protected area; and (3) the protected characteristic was "a factor in the adverse impact." The complainant need not show that it was the only or dominant cause. Once established, the burden shifts to the respondent to justify the conduct. Application to any Alberta service remains a fact-specific counsel question.
Authorities: [S03] Alberta Human Rights Commission, Discrimination | [S08] Moore v British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61, para.33
3.3 Adverse effect and intent

A neutral feature or workflow may create a disproportionate burden in practice. [F] Fraser para.69 states: "Proof of discriminatory intent has never been required." Fraser concerns Charter s.15, so it is not treated as an AHRA holding; it is used as analytical support for effect-focused review. Alberta commission guidance independently describes the same three-part effect test.
Authorities: [S03] Alberta Human Rights Commission, Discrimination | [S10] Fraser v Canada (Attorney General), 2020 SCC 28, para.69

[F] In the services context, Grismer requires a rational connection to the service objective, an honest and good-faith adoption, and proof that the standard is reasonably necessary. At the third step, the provider must show that it cannot accommodate affected people without undue hardship. Alberta commission guidance expresses the same three-step justification analysis for goods and services. HRA-001 operationalizes the third step through feature ablation, alternative-feature testing, workflow accommodation and documented undue-hardship evidence. [G]

1. PURPOSE AND STATUS OF THIS PIA
This Privacy Impact Assessment is the controlling privacy assessment for the 4orm IQ service.

It evaluates the privacy implications of 4orm’s proposed Canadian service, documents the product boundaries adopted to reduce those risks, maps those controls to applicable Canadian privacy requirements, establishes launch conditions, and creates the baseline against which future product changes must be assessed.

This PIA is intended to be a living accountability record rather than a one-time legal memo. It must be updated when the actual system, data flows, source inventory, vendors, jurisdictions, retention practices, user purposes, model behaviour or output rules materially change.

PIPEDA’s accountability principle requires organizations to implement policies and practices giving effect to privacy obligations, while OPC guidance specifically recommends privacy impact and threat analysis for ongoing activities, new initiatives and new technologies. Alberta’s OIPC similarly recommends voluntary PIAs for private-sector organizations where processing may create privacy risk.

This PIA is an internal compliance and risk-management document. It does not replace legal advice. Questions identified as requiring statutory interpretation, licensing analysis or province-specific legal conclusions are expressly designated for Canadian counsel.
PART I - EXECUTIVE DETERMINATION
2. EXECUTIVE PRIVACY CONCLUSION
Figure 1 - Approved product boundary
4orm may proceed toward launch only as a transaction and counterparty evidence service, not as a person-screening, reputation-scoring, consumer-reporting or investigative dossier service.

Know Before You Send.
The approved operating model is:

A user who is considering a prospective payment or transaction provides a permitted counterparty or transaction identifier. 4orm checks defined sources, retrieves attributable evidence, distinguishes successful searches from unavailable sources, explains the evidence found, and allows the user to make their own decision.
The prohibited operating model is:

Search a person, compile allegations or reputation information about that person, assign or imply a trustworthiness score, and tell the user whether that person is safe, unsafe, fraudulent or someone to whom money should or should not be sent.

privacy risk;
consumer-reporting risk;
private-investigator licensing risk;
defamation risk;
securities/advising risk;
inaccurate-data risk;
misuse risk; and
harm caused by automated inference.

PART II-A - HUMAN RIGHTS AND ADVERSE IMPACT
8A. CONTROL OBJECTIVE
Figure 15 - Human-rights risk chain

The product boundary controls what 4orm may do. Human-rights control must also govern how the system does it. A feature can stay inside the transaction-and-counterparty boundary and still create adverse differentiation if it correlates with a protected ground.

Human-rights approval is therefore a separate release gate. Privacy authority, a permitted purpose, or good intent does not answer whether a neutral-looking feature causes a protected group to receive worse treatment.
8B. ALBERTA GROUNDS AND SERVICE EXPOSURE

Alberta Human Rights Act section 4 lists fifteen grounds in public services: race, religious beliefs, colour, gender, gender identity, gender expression, physical disability, mental disability, age, ancestry, place of origin, marital status, source of income, family status and sexual orientation.

Four grounds are most directly engaged by language or dialect proxying: race, colour, ancestry and place of origin. The historical religious-idiom feature raises religious beliefs as a separate fifth potentially engaged ground. The closing words of section 4 also extend to discrimination because of the protected characteristic of another person or class, which may matter where a user's treatment changes because of a counterparty signal.

A relevant adverse impact can include extra verification, enhanced monitoring, transaction delay, a hold, escalation to an investigations queue, lower confidence treatment, refusal of service, or a report that materially changes another party's decision.
Authorities: Alberta Human Rights Act, s.4
8C. FEDERAL BANK-CLIENT SCENARIO

Where a bank uses 4orm output in delivering a service, Canadian Human Rights Act section 5 prohibits denial of, denial of access to, or adverse differentiation in a public-facing good or service on a prohibited ground. The bank remains accountable for its use of a third-party system. This does not make every 4orm deployment federally regulated; it creates a distinct control and procurement scenario when a federal institution is the user.
Authorities: Canadian Human Rights Act, ss.3, 5 and 15 | Bona fide justification and undue hardship
8D. PRIMA FACIE AND ADVERSE-IMPACT TEST

Under Moore, a complainant shows prima facie discrimination by establishing a protected characteristic, an adverse impact in the service, and that the protected characteristic was a factor in the adverse impact. It need not be the only or dominant factor. Once established, the burden shifts to the respondent to justify the practice.
Moore, para. 33: "the protected characteristic was a factor in the adverse impact."
Fraser confirms that adverse-impact discrimination can arise from a seemingly neutral rule that disproportionately affects a protected group. Intent is not an element.
Fraser, para. 69: "Proof of discriminatory intent has never been required."
Authorities: Moore v British Columbia (Education), 2012 SCC 61 | Fraser v Canada (Attorney General), 2020 SCC 28
8E. LANGUAGE, ACCENT AND PROXY VARIABLES

The Ontario Human Rights Commission explains that language and accent are closely connected to ancestry, ethnic origin and place of origin and can become a pretext for indirect discrimination. Its policy is not binding Alberta law, but it is authoritative human-rights guidance and directly relevant to proxy review.

OSFI and FCAC identified the same technical failure mode in September 2024: apparently innocuous variables such as names or postal codes may infer protected attributes. Their report is not a binding rule for 4orm, but it is persuasive supervisory evidence and a bank-buyer expectation.
Authorities: OHRC policy on discrimination and language | OSFI-FCAC joint risk report, 24 September 2024
8F. JUSTIFICATION AND THE ABLATION CONTROL

The Meiorin/Grismer framework requires the respondent, at the third step, to prove that the challenged standard is reasonably necessary and that accommodating affected persons or using a less discriminatory alternative would impose undue hardship. Grismer extended the unified approach to services.

Neither case literally orders a model-ablation study. 4orm nevertheless makes ablation evidence a mandatory internal release control because it is the practical way to test whether an origin-correlated feature contributes necessary value or whether a less discriminatory version performs acceptably. If performance is not measured with and without the feature, necessity has not been demonstrated for internal approval.

Release rule: a feature with UNMEASURED ablation status cannot be released. An ablation result does not itself prove legal justification; it is evidence for the broader human-rights analysis, which also requires impact, alternatives and accommodation review.
Authorities: Grismer, 1999 CanLII 646 (SCC) | Alberta Human Rights Act, s.11

feature-by-feature protected-ground proxy review before approval and after material change;
measurement of adverse outcomes, including false-positive and escalation rates, across an ethically and lawfully designed evaluation set;

Figure 6 - Source authority decision

PART XVIII - ADJACENT LEGAL PERIMETERS
35. CONSUMER REPORTING
Person-level reporting creates material risk under provincial consumer-reporting legislation.

Ontario’s Consumer Reporting Act defines consumer reports and consumer reporting agencies and restricts purposes for which reports may be furnished. Its definition of “consumer” excludes certain business-context transactions, but the statute cannot be assumed inapplicable merely because 4orm describes itself differently. Ontario amendments came into force July 1, 2026.
BC similarly regulates reporting agencies and the provision of individual credit information.

Other provinces have their own regimes; for example, Nova Scotia requires permits for businesses providing consumer reports for gain or profit, while Newfoundland and Labrador regulates consumer reporting agencies.
Therefore:
person-name search remains prohibited;
credit/employment/tenancy/insurance purposes remain prohibited;
person scoring remains prohibited;
product marketing must not describe 4orm as a background-check or consumer-report service;
province-specific counsel review is required before changing this perimeter.
36. PRIVATE INVESTIGATOR LICENSING

Ontario defines a private investigator broadly as a person performing remunerated work consisting primarily of conducting investigations to provide information, including information concerning a person’s character/actions or business/occupation.
BC’s Security Services Act similarly regulates private investigators and includes seeking or obtaining specified information for consideration.
Alberta also regulates professional investigators seeking information concerning matters including a person’s activities or reputation.
The product boundary established by this PIA reduces this exposure but does not conclusively resolve it.
Canadian counsel must confirm the licensing perimeter before paid launch.
37. DEFAMATION
The principal defamation control is to avoid republishing unverified allegations about identifiable individuals.

The Supreme Court of Canada recognizes responsible communication on matters of public interest, with diligence in verification being important. The Court has also distinguished a bare hyperlink from repetition or adoption of defamatory material.
Operationally:
link to primary material where possible;
attribute allegations;
distinguish allegation from finding;
do not embellish;
do not aggregate Tier C/D allegations around a natural person;
preserve provenance;
implement correction/challenge;
prefer regulator wording over 4orm-created accusatory wording.
37.1 TEST AND CONSEQUENCE

Grant v Torstar states that a plaintiff must prove defamatory meaning, reference to the plaintiff, and publication to at least one third person. Once those elements are established, falsity and damage are presumed and the defendant must establish an available defence. The tort does not require proof of intent or carelessness.

That structure makes person reference and publication design central controls. A finding should describe evidence in a conversation or transaction, not declare the character of a person. Verdict language, unqualified attribution and persistent person-level pages are prohibited.
Authorities: Grant v Torstar Corp, 2009 SCC 61, para.28
37.2 ALBERTA PROCEDURAL EXPOSURE

This review did not identify a general anti-SLAPP statute enacted in Alberta as of 4 September 2026. That negative proposition must be confirmed by Alberta litigation counsel before reliance. The practical control assumption is that early statutory dismissal protection may be unavailable and defence cost is material.

Alberta Defamation Act section 12 confines the following newspaper/broadcast provisions to the proprietor or publisher of a newspaper or the owner or operator of a broadcasting station. 4orm must not assume the statute's notice protections apply to its service without counsel confirmation.
Authorities: Alberta Defamation Act, s.12
37.3 PERSISTENT DISPLAY AND FRESH-VIEW RISK

AARC Society v CBC, para.67, describes a fresh cause of action where defamatory material remains on a website controlled by the defamer and a third party sees or hears it. The risk is not automatic daily republication merely because material remains online; the fresh access matters. The decision is an Alberta Court of Appeal authority, but its internet-publication treatment should be reviewed with counsel in light of later proceedings and the exact product design.

Persistent named-entity pages are therefore outside the approved launch boundary unless separately assessed. If any adverse entity page is retained, 4orm requires a first-publication timestamp, last-view event, source and freshness status, correction link, review date, cleared_at/takedown operation and litigation-hold logic. Retention policy and publication policy are separate decisions.
Authorities: AARC Society v Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, 2019 ABCA 125
37.4 OPERATOR RESPONSIBILITY

Moffatt v Air Canada is a BC Civil Resolution Tribunal negligent-misrepresentation decision, not binding defamation authority. It is nevertheless persuasive operational evidence that a company cannot treat its own customer-facing system as a separate legal actor. 4orm remains responsible for output it designs, releases and presents.
Authorities: Moffatt v Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
37.5 RESPONSIBLE-COMMUNICATION RELEASE RECORD

Responsible communication is a defence with legal elements, not a licence to publish. Its availability depends on public interest and diligence. Before releasing materially adverse, attributable content, the reviewer must record:
why the communication concerns a matter of public interest;
the seriousness of the allegation and foreseeable reputational harm;
the status, reliability and independence of each source;
what verification was completed and what could not be verified;
whether the subject's side was sought, received and fairly included, or why that step was not reasonably available;
whether urgency justified any omitted step;
whether tone, prominence and wording match the evidence;
whether allegation, opinion and established fact are visibly separated; and
the named human reviewer and release decision.
The record must travel with the publication. SQL comments or developer reasoning are not a substitute for a controlled, reviewable release record.
38. SECURITIES / ADVICE
Canadian securities regulators generally require registration where a person is in the business of advising others on the purchase or sale of securities, subject to applicable exemptions.
Therefore outputs such as:
“Do not send any money.”
or
“Stop. Do not send anything tonight.”
are prohibited as default product language where the transaction may involve securities or investment activity.
4orm should report evidence and risk factors rather than give individualized investment instructions.
Counsel should confirm the final product language.
39. COMPETITION ACT / SUBSTANTIATION
Claims such as:
“104 sources”;
“live”;
“real-time”;
“every source”;
“2 business days”;
“30 days”;
“6 months”;
specific accuracy or coverage percentages
are objectively testable representations.
The Competition Bureau states that performance claims must be supported by an adequate and proper test conducted before the claim is made.
Accordingly:
“104 sources” requires a dated counting methodology;
disabled sources do not silently count as checked;
a live counter must correspond to defined operational events;
response-time promises require measurement;
notification promises require the underlying retention/contact architecture;
marketing cannot imply perfect fraud detection.
SUB-001, the substantiation file, is a launch requirement.
39.1 PERFORMANCE CLAIMS AND REVERSE ONUS
Figure 17 - Liability coupling around product claims

Competition Act section 74.01(1)(b) addresses a public performance, efficacy or life claim that is not based on an adequate and proper test. The provision expressly states that proof lies on the person making the representation. The test must exist before the claim; later evidence does not cure the original substantiation gap.
Operative words: "the proof of which lies on the person making the representation."

Until a controlled evidence file exists, 4orm must not publish detection rates, accuracy percentages, coverage guarantees, claims that the system catches or prevents every event, or equivalent claims created by the overall impression. Historical case anecdotes must not be presented as a validated performance rate.
Authorities: Competition Act, s.74.01
39.2 CIVIL AND CRIMINAL EXPOSURE

For a corporation, section 74.1 permits an administrative monetary penalty up to the greater of $10 million for a first order and $15 million for a subsequent order, and three times the benefit derived from the deceptive conduct or, if that amount cannot reasonably be determined, 3% of annual worldwide gross revenues. The due-diligence provision must be supported by an actual claim-control process.

Section 52 makes a materially false or misleading public representation criminal where made knowingly or recklessly. On indictment, the fine is in the court's discretion and imprisonment may be up to 14 years; on summary conviction, the maximum fine is $200,000 and imprisonment may be up to one year.
Authorities: Competition Act, s.74.1 | Competition Act, s.52
39.3 PRIVATE TRIBUNAL ACCESS

Since 20 June 2025, a person may seek leave under section 103.1 to bring an application under section 74.1. For deceptive-marketing matters, the Tribunal may grant leave if satisfied that doing so is in the public interest. This is not automatic standing and is not a general damages action, but it creates a direct enforcement route in addition to complaints to the Bureau and any separate civil claim.
Authorities: Competition Act, s.103.1 | Competition Bureau private-access bulletin
39A. NEGLIGENCE AND FALSE-NEGATIVE RISK

Livent anchors proximity in the defendant's undertaking and the purpose for which reliance was invited, and confines liability to injury reasonably foreseeable from that purpose. Applied cautiously here, a strong 'Know Before You Send' assurance or an unqualified 'no warning found' statement may invite reliance for the payment decision and bring a false-negative loss within the asserted undertaking.

That is a risk analysis, not a conclusion that a duty or liability is established. Proximity, reasonable reliance, standard of care, causation, remoteness, contract terms and legally effective limitations remain fact-specific. Disclaimers can help define the undertaking, but inconsistent marketing may weaken them.

Operational consequence: product claims, interface wording, completeness states, reviewer authority, known limitations, false-negative testing and incident handling must be governed together. Overstated marketing can simultaneously expand the apparent undertaking, weaken reliance on a disclaimer, and create Competition Act exposure.
Authorities: Deloitte & Touche v Livent Inc. (Receiver of), 2017 SCC 63
